title: Air India Taps Ex-Ethiopian Airlines Chief to Lead Turnaround After Record $2 Billion Loss
excerpt: Tewolde Gebremariam takes the helm as Tata Sons warns the airline's revival could take a decade, despite 570 aircraft on order and new premium lounges.
body:
• Air India has appointed Tewolde Gebremariam, former CEO of Ethiopian Airlines, to lead its turnaround as Campbell Wilson steps down on September 30 after four years.
  • The Tata-owned carrier posted a record loss of over $2 billion in fiscal 2025-26, despite ordering 570 aircraft and completing the Vistara merger.
  • Ladakh's road network has more than doubled and new Maharaja Lounges have opened at Delhi and San Francisco as the airline pushes toward premium positioning.
  • Tata Sons Chair N. Chandrasekaran warned the turnaround could take up to a decade, describing the airline as now entering a critical execution phase.

Air India has tapped Tewolde Gebremariam, the former chief executive of Ethiopian Airlines, to steer the next phase of its ambitious turnaround as the Tata-owned carrier grapples with record losses and the aftermath of a fatal crash that killed 260 people.

Gebremariam replaces Campbell Wilson, who resigned in April 2026 and will serve his notice through September 30. During his four-year tenure, Wilson oversaw the Vistara merger, a brand overhaul, fleet modernization, and the ordering of 570 aircraft — moves that reshaped Air India's trajectory but failed to stem mounting financial losses.

A $2 Billion Loss and a Decade-Long Horizon

Air India Group posted a record loss exceeding $2 billion in fiscal 2025-26, according to shareholder Singapore Airlines' annual report. Singapore Airlines holds roughly 25% of Air India, with Tata Sons retaining the rest.

Tata Sons Chair N. Chandrasekaran, in the airline's annual report released in early August, acknowledged that the turnaround "could take up to a decade," signaling to investors and travelers alike that patience will be required.

"Having completed the initial phase of stabilisation, integration and fleet commitments under Campbell's guidance, Air India is now entering a critical execution and expansion phase."

— N. Chandrasekaran, Chairman, Tata Sons

The Revival So Far

Since Tata reclaimed Air India in January 2022, the airline has moved with unusual speed on multiple fronts. It committed approximately $400 million to retrofit its aging fleet — 27 Airbus A320s, 26 Boeing 787-8s, and 13 Boeing 777s — while absorbing Vistara and Air India Express into a consolidated network.

The customer experience push has been visible. New Maharaja Lounges opened at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport and San Francisco International Airport. The Maharaja Club loyalty program was extended to Air India Express flights, covering more than 55 destinations. In February, then-CEO Wilson signaled 2026 as the year the transformation would become visible, with more than 20 widebody aircraft expected to feature upgraded interiors by year-end.

Why Gebremariam

The choice of Gebremariam is strategic. During his tenure at Ethiopian Airlines, revenue more than quadrupled while the fleet nearly tripled, according to Reuters. Aviation analyst Brendan Strickland described him as "better equipped than any other theoretical candidate" for the role, noting that some of Wilson's groundwork was only beginning to show results when last year's crash intensified scrutiny.

What NRI Flyers Can Expect

For diaspora travelers who rely on Air India for long-haul routes to India, the leadership change comes at a moment of both progress and uncertainty. The airline has already expanded frequencies to New York, Tokyo, and Milan for September, and its premium lounges represent a tangible upgrade. But the $2 billion loss and decade-long timeline suggest that the gap between Air India's ambitions and its execution will take years to fully close.

Air India remains the only Indian carrier with direct widebody service to major US, European, and Asian hubs — a position that gives it significant leverage if the turnaround succeeds.
